sentences.nl: Mijn naam is Bart de Pau,, online docent Nederlands.

sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we Nederlandse zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar-2, les 26 en 27, over het gebruik van ‘hebben’ of ‘zijn’ in het perfectum.
sentences.en: Today we practice Dutch sentences with the grammar of #dutchgrammar-2, lessons 26 and 27, about the use of 'have' or 'be' in the perfect tense.

sentences.nl: Het is de laatste les van de Dutch Summer School.
sentences.en: It is the last lesson of the Dutch Summer School.

sentences.nl: De les is begonnen.
sentences.en: The class has started.

sentences.nl: Beste mensen, we hebben 2 weken hard gestudeerd.
sentences.en: Dear people, we have studied hard for 2 weeks.

sentences.nl: Hebben jullie veel geleerd? — Ja, mijn Nederlands is verbeterd.
sentences.en: Did you learn a lot? — Yes, my Dutch has improved.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Have you (plural) learned much? — Yes, my Dutch is improved.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hebben jullie veel geleerd?" uses the perfect tense, which is common for talking about past actions with relevance to the present. "Hebben" is the auxiliary verb, and "geleerd" is the past participle.  
• "Mijn Nederlands is verbeterd" uses the present perfect tense again, but with "is" as the auxiliary verb, common with verbs of change like "verbeteren" (to improve).  
• Example 1: "Hebben jullie het boek gelezen?" (Have you read the book?)  
• Example 2: "Mijn Frans is verbeterd door te oefenen." (My French has improved by practicing.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Hebben jullie de wedstrijd gewonnen?" (Did you win the match?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• N/A

sentences.nl: We hebben veel Nederlands met elkaar gepraat.
sentences.en: We spoke a lot of Dutch with each other.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• We have a lot Dutch with each other talked.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence is in the perfect tense, using "hebben" as the auxiliary verb and "gepraat" as the past participle.  
• "Met elkaar" means "with each other," indicating a reciprocal action.  
• Word order places the time phrase "veel Nederlands" (a lot of Dutch) before the past participle "gepraat."

Examples:
- We hebben samen gegeten. (We have eaten together.)
- Hij heeft met zijn broer gesproken. (He has spoken with his brother.)
- Zij hebben veel plezier gehad. (They have had a lot of fun.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• We hebben veel over het weer gepraat. (We have talked a lot about the weather.)

sentences.nl: En we zijn in het boek, van hoofdstuk 10 naar hoofdstuk 18 gegaan.
sentences.en: And we have gone in the book from chapter 10 to chapter 18.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And we are in the book, from chapter 10 to chapter 18 gone.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En" (And) is a conjunction used to connect clauses.  
• "we zijn gegaan" is the past tense of "gaan" (to go) in the perfect form, using the auxiliary "zijn" (to be) because it's a verb of movement.  
• "in het boek" specifies the location within the book where the action takes place.  
• "van... naar..." is a structure meaning "from... to..." indicating movement or transition between two points.

Extra phrases:  
• "We zijn naar het park gegaan." (We have gone to the park.)  
• "Van januari naar februari is het koud." (From January to February, it is cold.)  
• "Hij is van school naar huis gegaan." (He has gone from school to home.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• We zijn van het begin naar het einde gegaan. (We have gone from the beginning to the end.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
(No cultural note applicable.)

sentences.nl: We hebben dus 9 hoofdstukken gedaan.
sentences.en: So we did 9 chapters.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• We have thus 9 chapters done.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "We hebben" is the present perfect tense, indicating a completed action.  
• "Dus" is a conjunction here meaning "thus" or "so," often used to connect thoughts or indicate a conclusion.  
• The sentence structure follows a Subject-Verb-Object order with "gedaan" (done) as the past participle.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "We hebben al gegeten." (We have already eaten.)  
  - "Hij heeft dus gelijk." (So, he is right.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• We hebben dus de opdracht afgerond. (So, we have completed the assignment.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
•

sentences.nl: En jij Anika? — Ja, ik heb ook veel geleerd.
sentences.en: And you, Anika? — Yes, I learned a lot too.

sentences.nl: Maar niet alleen de taal.
sentences.en: But not only the language.

sentences.nl: Ik ben op veel interessante plekken geweest.
sentences.en: I have been to many interesting places.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I am on many interesting places been.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the present perfect tense ("ben geweest" - have been), which is common for expressing experiences.  
• "Op veel interessante plekken" translates to "on many interesting places," where "op" means "on" or "at" and is used as a preposition for location.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Ik ben in Amsterdam geweest." (I have been to Amsterdam.)  
  - "We hebben veel geleerd op school." (We have learned a lot at school.)  
  - "Zij zijn naar het museum geweest." (They have been to the museum.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik ben op zoek naar een nieuw avontuur. (I am looking for a new adventure.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, traveling and visiting different places is often seen as an enriching experience, similar to other Western cultures. The Netherlands, being a relatively small country, makes it easy and common for people to travel frequently within Europe.

sentences.nl: Ik ken nu het Nederlandse platteland een beetje beter.
sentences.en: I now know the Dutch countryside a little better.

sentences.nl: En jij Pablo? — Gisteravond was voor mij de beste avond.
sentences.en: And you Pablo? — Last night was the best night for me.

sentences.nl: Ik ben naar een kroeg geweest…, alleen, zonder de andere studenten.
sentences.en: I went to a pub... alone, without the other students.

sentences.nl: Daar heb ik een meisje ontmoet.
sentences.en: I met a girl there.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• There have I a girl met.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Daar" means "there" and often indicates location.  
• "Heb ik" is the present perfect tense of "hebben," meaning "I have." The auxiliary verb "heb" comes before the subject "ik" in this structure.  
• "Een meisje" means "a girl."  
• "Ontmoet" is the past participle of "ontmoeten," meaning "to meet."

Extra phrases:  
• Hier heb ik een boek gelezen. (Here I have read a book.)  
• Daar heeft hij een hond gezien. (There he has seen a dog.)  
• Waar heb jij dat gekocht? (Where have you bought that?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Daar heb ik mijn sleutels gevonden. (There I have found my keys.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Een Drents boerenmeisje? — Inderdaad!
sentences.en: A Drenthe farm girl? — Indeed!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A Drents farm girl? — Indeed!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een Drents boerenmeisje" is a noun phrase. "Drents" is an adjective derived from "Drenthe," a province in the Netherlands, indicating origin. "Boerenmeisje" is a compound noun made of "boer" (farmer) + "meisje" (girl).  
• "Inderdaad" is an adverb meaning "indeed" or "certainly," used for affirmation.  
• Example 1: "Een Fries paard? — Inderdaad!" (A Frisian horse? — Indeed!)  
• Example 2: "Een Nederlands gerecht? — Inderdaad!" (A Dutch dish? — Indeed!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een Limburgse vlaai? — Inderdaad!" (A Limburg pie? — Indeed!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Boerenmeisje" reflects a stereotypical image of a girl from a rural area, often associated with traditional values and simplicity. The use of regional adjectives like "Drents" highlights regional pride and identity within the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Ik heb de hele avond Nederlands met haar geoefend.
sentences.en: I practiced Dutch with her all evening.

sentences.nl: Ik ben tot 1 uur gebleven.
sentences.en: I stayed until 1 o'clock.

sentences.nl: Mijn Nederlands is verbeterd…, door jouw lessen, Marieke… maar ook door haar!
sentences.en: My Dutch has improved..., because of your lessons, Marieke... but also because of her!

sentences.nl: Nou… dat klinkt erg romantisch.
sentences.en: Well… that sounds very romantic.

sentences.nl: Nog meer liefdesverhalen misschien? — Wie van jullie heeft ook een romantische avond gehad? — Soliman kijkt naar Gianluca, maar hij zegt niets.
sentences.en: More love stories perhaps? — Which of you also had a romantic evening? — Soliman looks at Gianluca, but he says nothing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Yet more love stories maybe? — Who of you has also a romantic evening had? — Soliman looks at Gianluca, but he says nothing.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Nog meer" means "yet more" or "even more," used to ask if there are additional instances.  
• "Wie van jullie" translates to "Who of you," a common way to address a group.  
• "Heeft...gehad" uses the present perfect tense, a common tense for past actions with present relevance.  
• "Kijkt naar" means "looks at," using the preposition "naar" to indicate direction.  

Examples:  
- "Nog meer koffie misschien?" (More coffee maybe?)  
- "Wie van jullie heeft dit boek gelezen?" (Who of you has read this book?)  
- "Hij kijkt naar de schilderijen." (He looks at the paintings.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Nog meer vragen voor de docent misschien?" (Any more questions for the teacher maybe?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, direct questions like "Wie van jullie heeft...?" are common in conversational settings, encouraging group participation or response.

sentences.nl: En Xing? — Ook zij zwijgt.
sentences.en: And Xing? — She also remains silent.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And Xing? — Also she is silent.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ook zij zwijgt" uses inversion, where the subject "zij" follows the adverb "ook". This is common in Dutch to emphasize certain elements.  
• The verb "zwijgt" is the third-person singular present tense of "zwijgen" (to be silent).  
• Example: "Ook hij lacht." (Also he laughs.)  
• Example: "Ook wij komen." (Also we are coming.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "En Pieter? — Ook hij gaat." (And Pieter? — Also, he is going.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch conversation, it's common to use "ook" for emphasizing similarity or agreement with a previous statement or context.

sentences.nl: Beste studenten, vanavond is de laatste barbecue.
sentences.en: Dear students, tonight is the last barbecue.

sentences.nl: Dat wordt erg gezellig en misschien ook wel erg laat.
sentences.en: That will be very fun and maybe also very late.

sentences.nl: Maar… morgen moeten we al vroeg vertrekken.
sentences.en: But… we have to leave early tomorrow.

sentences.nl: Om half 10 moeten alle huisjes leeg zijn.
sentences.en: By 9:30, all the cabins must be empty.

sentences.nl: Zorg daarom dat je voor de barbecue, al je koffer hebt gepakt.
sentences.en: Therefore, make sure you have packed your suitcase before the barbecue.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ensure therefore that you before the barbecue, already your suitcase have packed.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zorg daarom" uses "zorgen" meaning "to ensure" or "to make sure," with "daarom" indicating "therefore" or "for that reason."  
• "dat je voor de barbecue" is a subordinate clause where "voor" means "before."  
• "al je koffer hebt gepakt" uses the present perfect tense, where "al" means "already" and "hebt gepakt" means "have packed."

• Examples:  
  - "Zorg dat je op tijd bent." (Make sure you're on time.)  
  - "Hij had al zijn huiswerk gedaan." (He had already done his homework.)  
  - "Voor het eten, moeten we de tafel dekken." (Before the meal, we need to set the table.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zorg ervoor dat je voor de vergadering je rapport hebt gelezen. (Make sure you've read your report before the meeting.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, barbecues are popular social gatherings, often held in gardens or parks during the warmer months. It’s common to prepare and pack in advance to ensure everything goes smoothly.

sentences.nl: Ruim alles op en gooi je afval weg.
sentences.en: Clean everything up and throw away your trash.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Clear everything up and throw your waste away.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The verb "ruim op" (clear up) is a separable verb. In imperative forms, the prefix "op" is placed after the verb.  
• "Gooi weg" (throw away) is another separable verb, functioning similarly to "ruim op."  
• "Je afval" (your waste) uses the possessive "je" to indicate ownership of the waste.  

Additional Examples:  
• Ruim je kamer op. (Clear up your room.)  
• Gooi de oude kranten weg. (Throw away the old newspapers.)  
• Maak je huiswerk af voor morgen. (Finish your homework for tomorrow.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ruim je spullen op voordat je naar buiten gaat. (Clear up your things before you go outside.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, there is a strong emphasis on cleanliness and organization, particularly in shared spaces. It is common to hear phrases like this in both homes and workplaces, promoting tidiness and respect for communal areas.

sentences.nl: En als je morgen een transfer wilt,, van het vakantiepark naar station Beilen,, boek dat dan vanmiddag bij de receptie voor 2 uur.
sentences.en: And if you want a transfer tomorrow from the holiday park to Beilen station, book it at the reception by 2 PM this afternoon.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And if you tomorrow a transfer want, from the holiday park to station Beilen, book that then this afternoon at the reception before 2 o'clock.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence starts with a conjunction "En" (And), which connects it to a previous idea.  
• "Als" (if) introduces a conditional clause, requiring inversion of subject and verb (je morgen een transfer wilt).  
• "Van het vakantiepark naar station Beilen" is a prepositional phrase indicating direction or origin and destination.  
• "Boek dat dan vanmiddag bij de receptie voor 2 uur" uses an imperative structure, instructing the listener to book by a certain time.  

Extra phrases:  
- "Als je tijd hebt, kom dan langs." (If you have time, come by.)  
- "Hij moet het rapport voor vrijdag afmaken." (He must finish the report by Friday.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Als je morgen naar Amsterdam wilt, koop dan vandaag je treinkaartje. (If you want to go to Amsterdam tomorrow, buy your train ticket today.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

sentences.nl: Ik heb het erg leuk gevonden om jullie les te geven.
sentences.en: I really enjoyed teaching you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I have it very nice found to you all lesson to give.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the present perfect tense ("heb gevonden") to express a completed action.  
• "Erg leuk" means "very nice" or "very enjoyable," and "leuk vinden" is an expression meaning "to find enjoyable."  
• "Om...te..." is a construction used to express purpose or intention, similar to "to" in English when followed by a verb.  
• "Jullie" refers to "you all" or "you (plural)."

Extra phrases:  
• "Ik heb het boek gelezen." (I have read the book.)  
• "Hij vindt het leuk om te reizen." (He likes to travel.)  
• "We hebben genoten van de vakantie." (We enjoyed the holiday.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik heb het altijd leuk gevonden om nieuwe mensen te ontmoeten." (I have always found it enjoyable to meet new people.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, expressing enjoyment in teaching or sharing activities is common in both professional and social contexts. It reflects a value placed on learning and community engagement.

sentences.nl: Jullie Nederlands is beter geworden.
sentences.en: Your Dutch has improved.

sentences.nl: Daar hebben jullie hard voor gewerkt.
sentences.en: You worked hard for that.

sentences.nl: En jullie waren ook een hele leuke groep!
sentences.en: And you were also a really nice group!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And you were also a very nice group!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En" is a conjunction meaning "and."  
• "Jullie" is the plural form of "you," used for addressing multiple people.  
• "Waren" is the past tense of "zijn" (to be) for plural subjects (you were).  
• "Ook" means "also," used to add information.  
• "Een hele leuke" is a phrase where "hele" intensifies "leuke," meaning "very nice." "Hele" is used for emphasis, similar to "very" in English.  
• "Groep" means "group" in Dutch.

Examples:  
– "Jullie waren heel behulpzaam." (You were very helpful.)  
– "Hij is een hele goede vriend." (He is a very good friend.)  
– "Zij waren ook op het feest." (They were also at the party.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Jullie zijn een hele hechte familie. (You are a very close-knit family.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
*No cultural note for this sentence.*

sentences.nl: Ik ben blij, dat jullie allemaal naar de zomerschool zijn gekomen.
sentences.en: I am glad that you all came to summer school.

sentences.nl: Ik zie jullie vanavond bij de barbecue.
sentences.en: I'll see you tonight at the barbecue.

sentences.nl: De studenten bedanken Marieke, en ze gaan hun koffers pakken.
sentences.en: The students thank Marieke, and they go to pack their suitcases.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The students thank Marieke, and they go their suitcases pack.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "De studenten bedanken Marieke" is a simple sentence with subject-verb-object order, which is typical in Dutch main clauses.  
• "ze gaan hun koffers pakken" includes a separable verb "pakken" (to pack) that is often used in combination with "gaan" (to go). The infinitive "pakken" goes to the end of the clause.  
• "en" is a coordinating conjunction that connects two main clauses.  

Extra phrases:  
• "Ik ga mijn tas inpakken." (I am going to pack my bag.)  
• "We bedanken de leraar voor zijn hulp." (We thank the teacher for his help.)  
• "Ze gaan naar de supermarkt." (They go to the supermarket.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De kinderen bedanken hun ouders, en ze gaan naar bed. (The children thank their parents, and they go to bed.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, it is customary to thank someone before leaving a gathering or after receiving help or a service. This is considered polite and shows appreciation.

sentences.nl: In de volgende aflevering zijn we bij de barbecue.
sentences.en: In the next episode, we are at the barbecue.

sentences.nl: Ik ben wel benieuwd, wat Martin en Marieke tegen elkaar gaan zeggen.
sentences.en: I am curious about what Martin and Marieke are going to say to each other.

sentences.nl: Tot dan!
sentences.en: Until then!

sentences.nl: Doei!
sentences.en: Bye!

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

anika.spelling: The open vowel 'a' in the first syllable is long, indicated by the IPA /aː/.
anika.fast: The final /a/ in 'anika' can be pronounced with a shorter, more central vowel sound in rapid speech.

heb.spelling: Heb is a monosyllabic word with a short vowel /ɛ/ followed by a voiced bilabial plosive /b/.
heb.fast: In rapid speech, the final /b/ in ‘heb ik’ might be pronounced as a flap or even omitted entirely before the following vowel.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

maar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable.
maar.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'maar ik' may be reduced or assimilated to the following vowel.

niet.spelling: The vowel 'ie' is pronounced as a long /iː/ sound.
niet.fast: In casual speech, the /t/ in 'niet' may become unreleased or assimilate to a following consonant.

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

tot.spelling: The word 'tot' follows the closed syllable pattern, resulting in a short vowel sound /ɔ/.
tot.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in 'tot' may become less aspirated or even assimilate with a following consonant.

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

dat.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in a closed syllable is represented by a single 'a'.
dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

dan.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable, typical for monosyllabic adverbs.
dan.fast: In rapid speech, 'dan ik' may have the /n/ assimilated to [ŋ] before a velar sound.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

allemaal.spelling: The sequence 'aa' indicates a long /aː/ sound.
allemaal.fast: In connected speech, the initial /ˈɑlə-/ often reduces to /ˈɑl-/.

aflevering.spelling: The prefix ‘af-’ indicates a separable prefix, showing a clear boundary with the root.
aflevering.fast: The initial /f/ of ‘aflevering’ may assimilate to a voiced [v] in connected speech, especially after voiced sounds.

wat.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in closed syllables.
wat.fast: In connected speech, 'wat' often reduces to /wət/ or even /wə/ before vowels.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.
